subjective.question: Why are protochordates not classified as true Chordata?
subjective.answer: Like the remaining subphylum of the chordates, the Vertebrata, the protochordates have a hollow dorsal nerve cord, gill slits, a stiff supporting rod (the notochord, the forerunner of the backbone). The protochordates differ chiefly from the vertebrates in not having a backbone. The organisms belonging to the Protochordata are generally known as the lower chordates. They don't form a 'proper' taxonomic group and are only classified as such for convenience purposes; however, they do form a major division of Chordata. They are also known as Acraniata because they lack a true skull. They are generally found in marine water. Their body is bilaterally symmetrical, triploblastic, and coelomated. At a certain stage of their lives, their body develops a long, rod-like structure for support called the notochord. They exhibit organ system level of organization. E.g., Herdmania, Amphioxus.

subjective.question: What are protochordates? Give their characteristics and classification.
subjective.answer: Protochordate is an informal category of organisms used to describe the invertebrates that are closely related to vertebrates. Characteristics of Protochordata (tunicates & amphioxus): They are generally found in marine water. Their body is bilaterally symmetrical, triploblastic, and coelomated. At a certain stage of their lives, their body develops a long, rod-like structure for support called the notochord. They exhibit organ system level of organization. E.g., Herdmania, Amphioxus. Classification: This group is composed of the Phylum Hemichordata and the Subphyla Urochordata and Cephalochordata.

subjective.question: What is Hemichordata? Describe its characteristics and classification.
subjective.answer: Hemichordates are marine, solitary, deuterostomate animals with a body divided into three regions: proboscis, collar, and trunk; the coelom is divided into three cavities. They are bilaterally symmetrical and triploblastic, with a true coelom present. The primitive notochord is restricted to the proboscis only, thus called the stomochord. The gut is straight or U-shaped with an anus. The nervous system is normally diffuse and variable. The circulatory system is open, and the blood has no color and corpuscles. The excretory organ is the glomerulus. They are filter feeders. The Hemichordata consist of four classes: Enteropneusta, Pterobranchia, Planctosphaeroidea and Graptolita. E.g., Cephalodiscus, Rhabdopleura.

subjective.question: Explain Class Enteropneusta (acorn worms) — general characters, feeding, digestion, nervous system, excretion and reproduction.
subjective.answer: General characters: Enteropneusts, or acorn worms (about 70 species), are solitary, wormlike, bilaterally symmetrical marine animals, often brilliantly coloured. They usually range in size between 10 and 40 cm, and most occupy U-shaped burrows in sandy and muddy substrates between the limits of high and low tides. The proboscis is a short, conical projection at the worm's anterior end; a ring-like collar is posterior to the proboscis; an elongate trunk is the third division of the body. A ciliated epidermis and gland cells cover acorn worms. The mouth is located ventrally between the proboscis and the collar. A variable number of pharyngeal slits, from a few to several hundred, are positioned laterally on the trunk. Feeding: Cilia and mucus assist acorn worms in feeding; detritus and other particles adhere to the mucus-covered proboscis and ciliary tracts form a mucoid string that enters the mouth. Digestion: The digestive tract is a simple tube; food is digested as diverticula of the gut, called hepatic sacs, release enzymes. At low tide, coils of fecal material, called castings, lie on the substrate at burrow openings. Nervous system: It is ectodermal in origin, lies at the base of the ciliated epidermis, and consists of dorsal and ventral nerve tracts and a network of epidermal nerve cells, called a nerve plexus; there are no major ganglia and sensory receptors are unspecialized. Excretion: Excretory wastes may be filtered through the glomerulus, into the coelom of the proboscis, and later released to the outside through one or two pores in the wall of the proboscis. Reproduction: Enteropneusts are dioecious; they normally reproduce sexually via external fertilization, and develop either directly or via tornaria larvae.

subjective.question: What is Phylum Chordata? Explain the characteristics of chordates.
subjective.answer: Chordata is a large phylum of animals that includes the vertebrates together with the sea squirts and lancelets. They are distinguished by the possession of a notochord at some stage during their development. Chordates are bilaterally symmetrical, deuterostomate animals. Four unique characteristics are present at some stage in development: notochord, pharyngeal slits or pouches, dorsal tubular nerve cord, and postanal tail. There is a presence of an endostyle or thyroid gland, a complete digestive tract, and a ventral, contractile blood vessel (heart). The phylum is named after the notochord. The notochord consists of a connective-tissue sheath that encloses cells; this arrangement gives the notochord some turgidity, which prevents compression along the anteroposterior axis, while at the same time the notochord is flexible enough to allow lateral bending. In most adult vertebrates, cartilage or bone partly or entirely replaces the notochord.

subjective.question: What is Subphylum Urochordata? Describe its characteristics and classification.
subjective.answer: The subphylum Urochordata constitutes a unique group of animals under the Phylum Chordata. The members of this subphylum exhibit a high degree of diversity in form, habit and habitat. They are called tail chordates and are the most primitive of the chordates. They are found in the marine environment. They are sessile and filter-feeders. They are also known as tunicates because their body is surrounded by a leathery sheath composed of tunicin (cellulose). They show retrogressive metamorphosis: the notochord appears in the larval stage in the tail of the larva and disappears in the adult. They are triploblastic, with a U-shaped gut; coelom is absent. They are hermaphroditic. Respiration occurs through gills. They have an incomplete closed circulatory system. The excretory organs are absent. They reproduce asexually by budding. E.g., tunicates or sea squirts. Classification: The members of Urochordata are classified under three classes: Ascidiacea, Thaliacea and Larvacea (Appendicularia).

subjective.question: What are ascidians (tunicates)? Describe their body organization, digestion, circulation, excretion and reproduction.
subjective.answer: Ascidiacea, commonly known as the ascidians, tunicates (in part), and sea squirts (in part), is a class in the subphylum Tunicata of sac-like marine invertebrate filter feeders. Ascidians are characterized by a tough outer 'tunic' made of a polysaccharide. Body organization: Tunicates derive their name from a thick extracellular body covering, called a tunic, that is made up of cellulose-like, complex sugars. The adult tunicate body is shaped like a small barrel with two large openings called siphons — the oral siphon (inlet for water, also serves as the mouth opening) and the atrial siphon (opening for excurrent water). The most obvious internal structures are a very large pharynx and a cavity, called the atrium, that surrounds the pharynx laterally and dorsally. Numerous pharyngeal slits called stigmata perforate the pharynx. Digestion: The digestive tract of adult tunicates continues from the pharynx and ends at the anus near the atrial siphon. Tunicates mainly eat phytoplankton, zooplankton, detritus and other small organisms in the water, which are filtered through the tunicate; they have cilia in the pharynx and they also produce mucus. During feeding, cells of a ventral, ciliated groove, called the endostyle, form a mucous sheath that traps food particles. Circulation: Tunicates have a well-developed heart and circulatory system. The heart is a double U-shaped tube situated just below the gut. One vessel from the heart runs anteriorly under the endostyle, and another runs posteriorly to the digestive organs and gonads. Blood flow through the heart is not unidirectional; the heart periodically changes the direction that it pumps blood. Instead of blood vessels, the heart pumps blood through a number of small pockets called sinuses. Excretion: Ammonia diffuses into water that passes through the pharynx and is excreted. Reproduction: Urochordates are monoecious. Gametes may be shed through the atrial siphon for external fertilization or eggs may be retained in the atrium for fertilization and early development. Although self-fertilization occurs in some species, cross-fertilization is the rule. Development results in the formation of a tadpole-like larva with all four chordate characteristics.

subjective.question: Explain Subphylum Cephalochordata — characteristics, feeding, digestion, circulation, excretion and reproduction.
subjective.answer: Members of the subphylum Cephalochordata are called lancelets. The cephalochordates consist of two genera, Branchiostoma (amphioxus) and Asymmetron, and about 45 species. They are distributed throughout the world's oceans in shallow waters that have clean sand substrates. Cephalochordates are small (up to 5 cm long), tadpole-like animals; they are elongate, laterally flattened, and nearly transparent. The notochord of cephalochordates extends from the tail to the head, giving them their name; most of its cells are muscle cells, making the notochord somewhat contractile. Feeding: Cephalochordates are filter feeders. During feeding, they are partially or mostly buried in sandy substrates with their mouths pointed upward. Ciliated, fingerlike projections, called cirri, hang from the ventral aspect of the oral hood and are used in feeding, forming a grid that keeps out large particles. Water is drawn into the mouth by the beating action of cilia on the gills, passes from the pharynx through pharyngeal slits to the atrium, and out of the body through the atriopore. Digestion: Digestion is both extracellular and intracellular. A diverticulum off the gut, called the midgut cecum, extends anteriorly. Circulation: Cephalochordates do not possess a true heart; contractile waves in the walls of major vessels propel blood. Excretion: Excretory tubules are modified coelomic cells closely associated with blood vessels, suggesting active transport of materials between the blood and excretory tubules. Reproduction: Cephalochordates are dioecious. Gametes are shed into the atrium and leave the body through the atriopore. External fertilization leads to a bilaterally symmetrical larva.

subjective.question: Discuss the phylogenetic relationships between hemichordates and chordates.
subjective.answer: Animals in the phyla Hemichordata and Chordata share deuterostome characteristics with echinoderms. Most zoologists, therefore, believe that ancestral representatives of these phyla were derived from a common, as yet undiscovered, triploblastic ancestor. The evolutionary relationships between the hemichordates and chordates are difficult to document with certainty. The dorsal tubular nerve cord and pharyngeal slits of hemichordates are evidence of evolutionary ties between these phyla. Synapomorphies that distinguish chordates from hemichordates include tadpole larvae, a notochord, a postanal tail, and an endostyle. The earliest echinoderms were probably sessile filter feeders. The lifestyle of adult urochordates suggests a similar ancestry (perhaps from a common ancestor with echinoderms) for chordates. The evolution of motile chordates from attached ancestors may have involved the development of a tadpole-like larva. Increased larval mobility is often adaptive for species with sedentary adults because it promotes dispersal.

subjective.question: Explain the phylogenetic relationships of fishes.
subjective.answer: Fishes are members of the chordate subphylum Vertebrata; thus, they have vertebrae that surround their spinal cord and provide the primary axial support. They also have a skull that protects the brain. Molecular evidence gathered by comparing gene similarities of cephalochordates and vertebrates suggests that the vertebrate lineage may go back about 750 million years, although this date has not been confirmed by fossil evidence. Recent cladistic analysis of vertebrate evolution indicates that a group of fishes called hagfishes are the most primitive vertebrates known (living or extinct). A group of ancient eel-like animals, the conodonts, are known from fossils that date back about 510 million years; recent evidence is bringing a growing number of zoologists to accept them as full-fledged vertebrates. It was present in the bony armor of a group of fishes called ostracoderms. Muscle blocks along the body wall suggest an active swimming existence; this evidence means that these 530 million-year-old animals located prey by sight and then pursued it through prehistoric seas. The importance of freshwater in the evolution of fishes is evidenced by the fact that over 41% of all fish species are found in freshwater, even though freshwater habitats represent only a small percentage (0.0093% by volume) of the earth's water resources.

subjective.question: How are fishes classified? What are Agnathans and Gnathostomes?
subjective.answer: Fishes are typically divided into three groups: superclass Agnatha (jawless fishes), class Chondrichthyes (cartilaginous fishes), and superclass Osteichthyes (bony fishes). The latter two groups are included within the infraphylum Gnathostomata, a category containing all jawed vertebrates. Agnatha is an infraphylum of jawless fish in the phylum Chordata, subphylum Vertebrata, consisting of both present (cyclostomes) and extinct (conodonts and ostracoderms) species. Among recent animals, cyclostomes are sister to all vertebrates with jaws, known as gnathostomes. Gnathostomes: The term derives from Greek (gnathos) 'jaw' + (stoma) 'mouth'. Gnathostome diversity comprises roughly 60,000 species, which accounts for 99% of all living vertebrates. In addition to opposing jaws, living gnathostomes have true teeth (lost in some) and paired appendages (pectoral and pelvic fins).

subjective.question: What are Osteichthyes and Chondrosteans?
subjective.answer: Osteichthyes, popularly referred to as the bony fish, are members of the class Osteichthyes characterized by having at least some bone in their skeleton and/or scales, a bony operculum covering the gill openings, and lungs or a swim bladder. Chondrostean (subclass Chondrostei) is any of approximately 30 species of primitive ray-finned bony fishes that inhabit marine and freshwater environments of North America and Eurasia. Chondrosteans make up one of the three major subdivisions of the superclass Actinopterygii, the other two being the holosteans and the teleosts.

subjective.question: Describe locomotion, nutrition, digestive system, circulation and respiration in fishes.
subjective.answer: Locomotion: Fins and body wall push against the incompressible surrounding water. Most fishes are arranged in a zigzag pattern. The forked shape of the caudal fin reduces surface area that could cause turbulence and interfere with forward movement. Nutrition: The earliest fishes were probably filter feeders and scavengers. Fish nutrition dramatically changed with the evolution of jaws. Most modern fishes are predators; some fishes feed on invertebrate animals. Digestive system: The fish digestive tract is similar to that of other vertebrates. The stomach stores large, often infrequent, meals and is the primary site for enzyme secretion. Sharks and other elasmobranchs have a spiral valve. Circulation: Closed circulatory system; the heart pumps blood; red blood cells contain hemoglobin. Blood flows from the venous system through the sinus venosus, the atrium, the ventricle, the conus arteriosus, and into the ventral aorta. Five afferent vessels carry blood to the gills. Respiration: Water contains less than 2.5% of the oxygen present in air. Fishes pass water across gill surfaces and extract the small amount of oxygen present in the water. Some fishes maintain water flow by holding their mouths open; this method is called ram ventilation. Gill filaments extend from each gill arch and are called pharyngeal lamellae.

subjective.question: Write a note on swim bladders and buoyancy regulation in fishes.
subjective.answer: Swim bladder: a gas-filled sac present in the body of many bony fishes, used to maintain and control buoyancy. Teleosts have swim bladders. Buoyancy regulation in fishes: While modern fishes can regulate buoyancy by secreting gases from the blood into the swim bladder, primitive fishes, such as sturgeons, lack this secretion mechanism and rely entirely on air gulped at the surface to inflate the swim bladder. The blood secretes gases into the swim bladder in a vascular network called the rete mirabile ('miraculous net').

subjective.question: Describe excretion, osmoregulation and reproduction in fishes.
subjective.answer: Excretion: The primary excretory organ in fishes, as in other vertebrates, is the kidney. In fishes some excretion also takes place in the digestive tract, skin, and especially the gills (where ammonia is given off). Excretory structures in the kidneys are called nephrons. Osmoregulation: Osmoregulation is the process of maintaining an internal balance of salt and water in a fish's body. A fish is, after all, a collection of fluids floating in a fluid environment, with only a thin skin to separate the two. Reproduction: In most cases, the female drops eggs in the water which are immediately fertilized by sperm from the male. Another way is for fertilization to occur within the female's body before she drops them into the water. With the third and final method, the female retains the eggs within her body and the young are born alive. Development: Fish eggs hatch into larvae that are different from the adult form of the species. A larva swims attached to a large yolk sac, which provides the larva with food. The larva eventually goes through metamorphosis and changes into the adult form.

subjective.question: What are amphibians? Give their characteristics, phylogeny and classification.
subjective.answer: Amphibians are small vertebrates that need water, or a moist environment, to survive. The species in this group include frogs, toads, salamanders, and newts. All can breathe and absorb water through their very thin skin. Amphibians also have special skin glands that produce useful proteins. Characteristics: Amphibians are vertebrates; their skin is smooth and slimy; amphibians breathe through their skin, as well as their lungs in some cases; amphibians are cold-blooded; they have a complex life cycle (larval and adult stages); many species of amphibians vocalize, e.g., the chorus frog; some species fertilize eggs externally, some internally. Phylogeny: Amphibians evolved about 365 million years ago from a lobe-finned fish ancestor. As the earliest land vertebrates, amphibians were highly successful for more than 100 million years until reptiles took over as the dominant land vertebrates. Order Labyrinthodontia is also known as 'Stem Amphibia'. Classification: They are classified into three orders: frogs and toads (Anura), salamanders and newts (Caudata), and caecilians.

subjective.question: Describe the orders Anura and Caudata of amphibians.
subjective.answer: Order Anura (Salientia): Tail absent in adult; eyelids and tympanum present; skin scaleless and loose; further divided into five suborders — Amphicoela, Opisthocoela, Procoela, Diplasiocela etc. E.g., Frog and Toad. Members of the family Salamandridae are commonly called newts. The male grasps the female in a position called amplexus. Amphibian development includes larval stages called tadpoles; tadpoles often differ from the adults. Order Caudata: Members of the order Caudata are the salamanders. Tail present throughout life; pairs of legs relatively unspecialized; approximately 115 of the 350 described species of salamanders live in North America. Most live in moist forest-floor litter.

subjective.question: Describe external structure and locomotion in amphibians.
subjective.answer: Amphibians are the first true tetrapods, or vertebrates with four limbs. Amphibians breathe with gills as larvae and with lungs as adults. They have a three-chambered heart and a relatively complex nervous system. Supportive processes called zygapophyses on each vertebra prevent twisting. The first vertebra is a cervical vertebra and the last trunk vertebra is a sacral vertebra. Sternum is present in the anterior ventral trunk region. Unlike other vertebrates, amphibians have contractile vessels, called lymphatic hearts. Locomotion on land is by walking and the tail often swings from side to side or is used as a prop, particularly when climbing.

subjective.question: Describe nutrition and the digestive system of amphibians.
subjective.answer: Most adult terrestrial and aquatic amphibians feed on invertebrates (animals that do not have backbones), including earthworms, bloodworms, black worms, white worms, tubifex worms, springtails, fruit flies, fly larvae, mealworms, and crickets. The amphibian gastrointestinal tract is simple (short and without a cecum); digestion is enzymatic (e.g., pepsinogen), and peristalsis (muscular action) and ciliary action move food through the system. The stomach of amphibians is low in pH (acidic) and the enzyme pepsinogen is converted to pepsin to break down proteins into amino acids.

subjective.question: Describe circulation, gas exchange and temperature regulation in amphibians.
subjective.answer: Amphibians have two circulatory routes: one for oxygenation of the blood through the lungs and skin, and the other to take oxygen to the rest of the body. The blood is pumped from a three-chambered heart with two atria and a single ventricle. Respiratory gas exchange is conducted through the thin, gas-permeable skin and the gills. Gas exchange across the skin is called cutaneous respiration. Amphibians and reptiles are ectotherms that control their body temperature through external sources such as basking in the sun to warm up.

subjective.question: Describe the nervous and sensory functions of amphibians.
subjective.answer: The nervous system is basically the same as in other vertebrates, with a central brain, a spinal cord, and nerves throughout the body. The amphibian brain is relatively simple but broadly the same structurally as in reptiles, birds and mammals. The forebrain contains olfactory centers and regions that regulate color change and visceral functions. The midbrain contains a region called the optic tectum; the midbrain also processes visual sensory information. The lower eyelid is movable, and cleans and protects the eye; much of it is transparent and is called the nictitating membrane. A fold of epithelium called the iris surrounds the pupil. Abutting the tympanic membrane is a middle-ear ossicle (bone) called the stapes (columella), and a second ossicle, called the operculum, connects the pectoral girdle to the inner ear.

subjective.question: Describe excretion and osmoregulation in amphibians.
subjective.answer: Although amphibians are formally given the status of terrestrial animals, they are poorly adapted to life on land. They excrete nitrogen in the form of urea and cannot produce urine more concentrated than the blood. Their skins are permeable to water. Fluid and electrolyte homeostasis in amphibians is maintained by a fine balance of the activity of the kidneys, urinary bladder and skin. In these animals, the kidneys produce copious volumes of dilute urine, and the bladder serves mostly as a reservoir of water during terrestrial activity.

subjective.question: Describe reproduction, development, metamorphosis and parental care in amphibians.
subjective.answer: Amphibians reproduce sexually with either external or internal fertilization. Development includes three stages: egg, larva, and adult. Frogs are not the only animals to undergo metamorphosis; most other amphibians also undergo remarkable changes throughout their life cycles, as do many species of invertebrates. Metamorphosis in amphibians is the transformation of the larva to a miniature adult replicate, and usually from an aquatic to a terrestrial or semi-terrestrial lifestyle. Metamorphosis marks the beginning of the end of larval life. Parental care: Among amphibians, parental care includes attendance of the eggs, transportation of eggs or larvae, and feeding of larvae. Parental care is associated with only those species that place their eggs in single clusters, never with those that scatter their eggs in aquatic situations.

subjective.question: What are reptiles? Give their characteristics and describe the orders Testudines, Rhynchocephalia and Squamata.
subjective.answer: Reptiles are air-breathing vertebrates covered in special skin made up of scales, bony plates, or a combination of both. They include crocodiles, snakes, lizards, turtles, and tortoises. Characteristics of reptiles: Reptiles are vertebrates; they have backbones; their bodies are completely covered with scales; they are cold-blooded; reptiles produce shelled eggs or bear live young; all species fertilize eggs internally; all species of reptiles have at least one lung. All reptiles periodically shed the outer, epidermal layers of the skin in a process called ecdysis. A plate of bone, called the secondary palate, evolved in the archosaurs and separates the nasal and mouth passageways. Order Testudines (Testudinata): Testudinata is the group of all tetrapods with a true turtle shell. It includes both modern turtles and many of their extinct, shelled relatives. Order Rhynchocephalia: Order Rhynchocephalia is the sister group to the order Squamata, and rhynchocephalids (sphenodontids) share numerous traits with squamates. Both groups possess a transverse cloacal opening (the vent), teeth that are attached superficially to the jawbones, and fracture planes in the tail vertebrae. Order Squamata: Squamata is the largest order of reptiles, comprising lizards, snakes, and amphisbaenians, which are collectively known as squamates or scaled reptiles. The skin of amphisbaenians has ringlike folds called annuli.
